blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Use rhetorical devices with control to persuade a named audience; keep the tone persuasive rather than ranting.

blocks.heading: Counterargument, rebuttal, concession
blocks.text: A counterargument is the position that opposes yours; a rebuttal is your answer to it; a concession is the part of it you admit is right before you answer the rest. The three work as a sequence: the counterargument is voiced fairly, the concession pays it its due, and the rebuttal answers what remains — which is why an argument that concedes nothing convinces nobody, and an argument that concedes everything has already stopped.

blocks.heading: Why concessions convince
blocks.text: A concession followed by a rebuttal makes an argument more convincing because the reader is shown fairness before they are shown the answer: the admission earns the trust the reply spends. "It is true that the new road will take the old trees, and the old trees matter — and the flooding that the road prevents will take more of them, root and bank" — the reader who loved the trees has been met, and then given a reason they can weigh rather than a verdict they must resist. Placing the counterargument beside the point, and answering it there, lets the reader watch the case survive its strongest test.

blocks.heading: Repetition in argument’s clothing
blocks.text: Repeating the same point in new words is not developing it: development adds reason, example or consequence, and an argument that repeats merely occupies the words its development needed. "Homework is stressful, and stress is what homework causes" has said one thing twice; the paragraph’s real work — who is stressed, how much, compared with what — has not begun. The cure is the addition test: what did the second sentence add? If the answer is only phrasing, the paragraph is repeating, and its development is still owed.

blocks.heading: Rhetorical force, from devices
blocks.text: Tricolon and anaphora add force to an argument because rhythm carries conviction: a list of three completes a thought with a beat the reader can agree to, and a repeated opening makes the points feel like a single pressure rather than a pile. Inclusive pronouns — we, us, our — build common ground with an audience: the reader is made a member of the case rather than its target, and the member argues with you while the target argues back. The devices are used sparingly and aimed: one tricolon per section, placed where the case turns.

blocks.heading: Force against rant
blocks.text: Persuasive force and a ranting or accusing tone are opposites: force argues the case, and a rant relieves the writer. The reader of a rant defends themselves — checking the case for faults instead of weighing it — and the audience the piece was written to hold becomes the audience the piece has attacked. The line between them is the second person: "you have ignored" accuses, and "we have not yet asked" recruits; the same evidence, the same numbers, lands on opposite sides of the reader’s defences.

blocks.heading: Worked example: the accused sentence repaired
blocks.text: A draft sentence: "You have all sat by while the library fell apart, and you should be ashamed." What it accuses the reader of — sitting by — is the one thing the reader will now argue about, and the piece’s evidence is suddenly on trial. The repair: "The library fell apart while the town was busy, which is not a charge — it is what happens to shared things when nobody is asked to share. We are the ones who can ask." The evidence stays, the shame goes, and the reader who was the target becomes the membership the argument needs.

blocks.heading: Judging an argument’s strength
blocks.text: Judging how convincing an argument paragraph is means asking what it overlooks: the strongest case is the one whose omissions you had to search for, not the one that never looked. The moves are three: name the paragraph’s claim and its evidence; ask which of the reader’s doubts it has not met; weigh whether the unmet doubt defeats the claim or merely qualifies it. A paragraph can be well written and unconvincing — the sentences polished, the objection unmet — and the judgement says which.
